pos: n. (a spreading disease of the skin rendering a man ceremonially unclean; rendering Hebrew tsaraath, Greek lepra)
etymology: From the Greek lepra, from lepis, a scale. Hebrew tsaraath covers a range of spreading conditions, and is used of garments and house walls as well as skin, so the biblical category is wider than the modern medical diagnosis.
biblical_def: Leprosy in Scripture is a disease with a liturgy attached, and the liturgy is what the Bible is chiefly interested in. The law puts the leper outside and gives him words to say: “his clothes shall be rent, and his head bare, and he shall put a covering upon his upper lip, and shall cry, Unclean, unclean” (Leviticus 13:45). He wears the signs of mourning and announces his own condition — a man required to preach the doctrine of sin with his body. It is no respecter of rank: Naaman was “a great man with his master, and honourable… a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” (2 Kings 5:1), and the whole force of that verse is the last clause. It also passes to the greedy: Gehazi is told, “The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow” (2 Kings 5:27). Against all this stands one sentence in the Gospels: “Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matthew 8:3). Under the law, touching a leper made the toucher unclean. Here the traffic runs the other way, and the touch is not a lapse but the point — a man who had not been touched in years is touched first and healed second.
webster_summary: A spreading uncleanness that put a man outside the camp crying Unclean, unclean. It spares neither rank nor prophet's servant — and Christ heals it by the one gesture the law forbade, a touch.
webster_full: LEPROSY, n. [from leprous; Gr. lepra, from lepis, a scale.] A foul cutaneous disease, appearing in dry, white, thin, scurfy scabs, attended with violent itching.
2. It sometimes covers the whole body, rarely the face. It is called also elephantiasis.
3. LEPROUS, a. Infected with leprosy; covered with white scales.
4. LEPER, n. A person affected with leprosy.
5. In Scripture, leprosy was a ceremonial as well as a bodily uncleanness, and the leper was separated from the congregation, Lev. 13.
corruption_summary: The laws of Leviticus 13 are dismissed as primitive quarantine, so that the doctrine they teach is lost — and the cleansing of lepers is read as mere kindness rather than as the Messiah's credential.
corruption_paragraphs: Reading Leviticus 13 as ancient public health explains the isolation and misses everything else. Sanitation does not require rent clothes, a bare head, a covered lip, and a cry of Unclean, unclean; those are the marks of mourning and confession. Nor does it explain a law of leprosy in garments and in the walls of a house, which no infection theory accounts for. The chapters teach by the body what sin is: it spreads, it defiles what it touches, it puts a man outside the camp, and no ritual is prescribed for curing it — the priest can only diagnose. The whole apparatus exists to make a man long for a cleansing the law could describe and never supply.

The principle to recover is why cleansed lepers mattered so much in the Gospels. When John's disciples came asking whether Jesus was the one that should come, the answer given was a list, and the lepers are cleansed stood in it beside the blind seeing and the dead being raised (Matthew 11:5). Leviticus 14 contains an elaborate ritual for the cleansing of a leper that Israel had almost no occasion to perform, because such cleansings did not happen. When they began to happen, the priests had to open a book that had lain shut. And the manner of it — I will; be thou clean — answers the leper's cautious if thou wilt, thou canst with the two words he had not dared to assume.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaraath is a spreading scaly affliction of skin, cloth, or wall, rendering unclean. Greek lepra is leprosy; katharizo, to cleanse, is the verb used of its removal.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaraath (H6883) — leprosy; used of persons, garments, and the walls of a house.
Hebrew metsora (H6879) — a leper, one struck with the plague; the participle of being smitten.
Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be unclean; the state the leper announced of himself.
Greek lepra (G3014) — leprosy; from lepis, a scale.
Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse, make clean; the lepers are cleansed, Matthew 11:5.
usage: Of the leper's required cry: shall cry, Unclean, unclean (Leviticus 13:45).
Of rank that could not exempt: a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper (2 Kings 5:1).
Of the forbidden touch that healed: Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him (Matthew 8:3).

pos: v. (to make unclean, to pollute; rendering Hebrew tame, Greek koinoo and miaino)
etymology: From Old French defouler, to trample, crossed with the Saxon fylan, to make foul. Greek koinoo is instructive: it means to make common, so that to defile a thing is to strip it of its separateness — the opposite of sanctifying.
biblical_def: To defile is to make unclean, and our Lord fought his sharpest battle over the direction the defilement travels. The Pharisees held that uncleanness entered from outside, through unwashed hands and forbidden foods. He denied it: “Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man” (Matthew 15:11), and Mark records the conclusion baldly: “That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man” (Mark 7:20). The list that follows — evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies — locates the source in the heart, and Mark adds the editorial note that in saying this he was purging all meats. Paul applies the word to the church as a building: “If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” (1 Corinthians 3:17) — a warning aimed at men splitting a congregation into parties. And Hebrews names the mechanism by which one man's bitterness spreads: “lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled” (Hebrews 12:15). A root works underground, appears late, and by the time it is visible it has already fed on a good deal of soil.
webster_summary: To make unclean — in Greek, to make common. Christ reverses the assumed direction: defilement comes out of a man, not into him. Paul warns against defiling the church, and Hebrews against the root of bitterness.
webster_full: DEFILE, v.t. [Sax. fylan, to make foul.] To make unclean; to render foul or dirty; in a general sense.
2. To make impure; to render turbid; as, to defile a stream.
3. To soil or sully; to tarnish; as reputation.
4. To pollute; to make ceremonially unclean, as by the touch of a dead body.
5. To corrupt chastity; to debauch; to violate.
corruption_summary: Defilement is treated as environmental — a matter of what a man is exposed to rather than what proceeds from him — which is precisely the Pharisaic error Christ overturned.
corruption_paragraphs:
Mark 7 records the argument and it recurs in every generation. The Pharisees had built a fence of external observances on the assumption that holiness is preserved by controlling contact, and our Lord's answer went to the root: nothing entering from outside can defile the heart, because it does not enter the heart. The instinct survives in two forms today. One is a Christian version that measures faithfulness by separation — what is avoided, watched, read, and eaten — and can produce a scrupulous person with an untouched heart. The other is the secular version, which explains wrongdoing entirely by environment and upbringing, and therefore locates the cure in changing conditions. Both agree that the trouble comes from outside. Christ says it comes out.

This is not an argument against prudence; a man who knows his own heart will avoid what provokes it. But avoidance is a strategy, not a cleansing, and no arrangement of circumstances has ever changed what proceeds from within.

The principle to recover is that the remedy must therefore be a new heart. If defilement came from outside, better fences would suffice; because it comes from the heart, only regeneration answers it. Ezekiel promises exactly this — a new heart and a new spirit, the stony heart taken away. And Hebrews 12:15 shows the practical shape of the doctrine in a congregation: the church is told to look diligently, because a root of bitterness is not visible at first and defiles many by the time it is. Watching over one another is not intrusion; it is the ordinary means by which God keeps a body clean.
roots_summary: Hebrew tame is to be or become unclean. Greek koinoo is to make common, the opposite of setting apart; miaino is to stain or pollute.
roots_lines: Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be unclean, to defile; the standard term of the Levitical law.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to make common; used of profaning the sabbath and the sanctuary.
Greek koinoo (G2840) — to make common, to defile; the verb of Matthew 15:11 and Mark 7:20.
Greek miaino (G3392) — to stain, to pollute; used of conscience and mind defiled, Titus 1:15.
Greek phtheiro (G5351) — to corrupt, to destroy; the verb behind defile the temple, 1 Corinthians 3:17.
usage: Of the direction of defilement: that which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man (Mark 7:20).
Of the church as a temple: if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy (1 Corinthians 3:17).
Of bitterness spreading: lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you (Hebrews 12:15).
scriptures: Mark 7:20
And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man.
Matthew 15:11
Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.
1 Corinthians 3:17
If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.
Hebrews 12:15
Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled;

pos: a. and pp. (made unclean, profaned; chiefly of worship and of a city; rendering Hebrew gaal and chalal)
etymology: From the Latin polluo, to soil or defile, from por- and luo, to wash away in the sense of befouling. In the KJV the word attaches most often not to individuals but to altars, offerings, sabbaths, and cities — the public things.
biblical_def: Polluted in the Authorized Version is chiefly a word about worship gone bad while continuing on schedule. Malachi opens the indictment: “Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible” (Malachi 1:7). The priests are not accused of abandoning the sacrifices but of bringing what cost them nothing, and their reply — wherein? — shows they had lost the ability to see it. The prophet repeats the charge: “ye have profaned it, in that ye say, The table of the LORD is polluted” (Malachi 1:12). Ezekiel traces the failure to its office: “Her priests have violated my law, and have profaned mine holy things: they have put no difference between the holy and profane, neither have they shewed difference between the unclean and the clean” (Ezekiel 22:26). The priest's work was to teach a distinction, and when he stops making it the whole people lose the category. And Zephaniah turns the word on a city: “Woe to her that is filthy and polluted, to the oppressing city!” (Zephaniah 3:1) — the pollution named there is oppression, so that injustice in the streets and defiled worship at the altar are one condition described twice.
webster_summary: Made unclean or profaned — chiefly of altars, offerings, and cities. Malachi's priests offer polluted bread and cannot see it; Ezekiel's put no difference between holy and profane; Zephaniah calls an oppressing city polluted.
webster_full: POLLUTE, v.t. [L. polluo.] To defile; to make foul or unclean; in a general sense.
2. To defile, in a religious sense; to render ceremonially unclean; to profane.
3. To violate by illegal sexual commerce; to debauch.
4. POLLUTED, pp. Defiled; rendered unclean; profaned.
5. POLLUTION, n. The act of polluting; defilement; uncleanness; impurity.
corruption_summary: Worship is judged by its effect on the worshipper rather than by whether God accepts it — and the priestly duty of distinguishing holy from profane is abandoned as a failure of welcome.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 22:26 names the office in one clause: the priests were to put difference between the holy and profane. That work of distinguishing is the first casualty wherever the chief aim of a service becomes accessibility. The reasoning is always kind — distinctions exclude, and exclusion drives people away — and its result is a congregation with no working category of holiness, which cannot then be taught anything about sin, atonement, or the fear of God. The regulative principle of worship exists to keep this from happening: what God has commanded in his worship is required, and what he has not commanded is not permitted. It is not a preference for austerity but a refusal to let the church decide for itself what pleases God. Malachi's priests are the sharper warning, because everything looked functional. The altar was in use, the bread was offered, the schedule was kept; the fault was in what was brought, and in the settled contempt underneath it. Their question, wherein have we polluted thee?, is what conscience sounds like once it has stopped working.

The principle to recover is Zephaniah's joining of the altar and the street. He calls the city filthy and polluted, and the sins he lists are oppression, disobedience, and refusal of correction — not liturgical faults. Scripture will not let a congregation be careful about worship and careless about justice, or the reverse. Isaiah 1 makes the same point at greater length: God is weary of solemn assemblies offered by hands full of blood. Pure worship and clean dealing are one obedience, and God receives them together or not at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew gaal is to defile or stain; chalal is to profane, to treat as common. Both are used of altars, sabbaths, and holy things rather than chiefly of private conduct.
roots_lines: Hebrew gaal (H1351) — to defile, to pollute; the polluted bread of Malachi 1:7.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to make common; used of the sabbath, the name, and the sanctuary.
Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be unclean; the general Levitical term for defilement.
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, that which is set apart; the category the priests failed to teach.
Greek alisgema (G234) — pollution, contamination; pollutions of idols, Acts 15:20.
usage: Of offerings that cost nothing: ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar (Malachi 1:7).
Of the lost distinction: they have put no difference between the holy and profane (Ezekiel 22:26).
Of an oppressing city: woe to her that is filthy and polluted, to the oppressing city! (Zephaniah 3:1).

pos: n. (a defect or flaw disqualifying an offering or a priest; rendering Hebrew mum, Greek amomos in the negative)
etymology: From Old French blemiss-, to make pale or to wound. Hebrew mum is a spot or bodily defect; the Greek adjective amomos, without blemish, becomes one of the New Testament's standard words for the church's final state.
biblical_def: A blemish in the law is any defect that disqualifies, and it governs both what is offered and who offers it. Of the offering: “whatsoever hath a blemish, that shall ye not offer: for it shall not be acceptable for you” (Leviticus 22:20). God does not receive damaged goods, and the rule closed off the natural temptation to give the animal that was going to be lost anyway. Of the priest: “Whosoever he be of thy seed in their generations that hath any blemish, let him not approach to offer the bread of his God” (Leviticus 21:17) — a hard statute, and it was never a judgment on the man's worth, since the same chapter provides that he shall eat of the holy things. What it taught was that the priesthood pictured a perfection no son of Aaron had. Peter draws the line to its end: we were redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19) — the unblemished victim at last, who is also the unblemished priest. And Paul carries it forward to the church: Christ will “present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27). The bride is made what the offering had to be.
webster_summary: A disqualifying defect. No blemished offering was acceptable and no blemished priest might approach — teaching a perfection Aaron's sons lacked, supplied at last by a lamb without blemish and given to the church.
webster_full: BLEMISH, v.t. [Fr. blemir, to blast, to fade.] To mark with any deformity; to injure or impair any thing which is well formed.
2. To tarnish, as reputation or character; to defame.
3. BLEMISH, n. Any mark of deformity; any scar or defect that diminishes beauty.
4. Reproach; disgrace; that which impairs reputation; taint; turpitude.
5. In Scripture, a bodily defect which disqualified for the priesthood or for sacrifice, Lev. 21.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 21 is read as contempt for the disabled, and the sacrificial standard is softened — when the law honoured the blemished priest's portion and pointed past every son of Aaron to a spotless one.
corruption_paragraphs: The exclusion of blemished priests in Leviticus 21 is frequently cited as evidence that Scripture despises the disabled, and the charge collapses on the text itself. The disqualified man is not cast out, not shamed, and not deprived: He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy (Leviticus 21:22). He keeps his birthright, his provision, and his place among his brethren; what he may not do is one particular symbolic act. The whole priesthood was a picture, and a picture with a flaw in it teaches the wrong thing. Scripture's regard for the afflicted is not in question elsewhere — it forbids cursing the deaf and putting a stumblingblock before the blind, and the Lord's own ministry was largely spent among the maimed.

The principle to recover is that the standard was never lowered; it was met. Malachi's generation tried lowering it, bringing the blind and the lame for sacrifice, and God's answer was to ask whether their governor would accept such a gift. The law held the bar at without blemish for fifteen hundred years without one offering that truly satisfied it, until Peter could write of a lamb without blemish and without spot. And Ephesians 5:27 completes the movement: what Christ requires he supplies, and the church that had every blemish is the one he presents to himself holy and without blemish, having washed her with the water by the word.
roots_summary: Hebrew mum is a spot or bodily defect disqualifying an offering or a priest; tamim, its opposite, means whole, complete, without blemish. Greek amomos is blameless, unblemished.
roots_lines: Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, a bodily defect; the disqualifying flaw of Leviticus 21-22.
Hebrew tamim (H8549) — whole, complete, without blemish; required of every offering.
Hebrew qorban (H7133) — an offering, that which is brought near; what the blemish disqualified.
Greek amomos (G299) — without blemish, faultless; of Christ, and of the church presented to him.
Greek aspilos (G784) — without spot, unstained; paired with amomos in 1 Peter 1:19.
usage: Of the offering's standard: whatsoever hath a blemish, that shall ye not offer (Leviticus 22:20).
Of the priest disqualified: that hath any blemish, let him not approach (Leviticus 21:17).
Of the church made spotless: holy and without blemish (Ephesians 5:27).

pos: a. (not circumcised; outside the covenant sign; figuratively, unyielding — of the heart, ears, or lips; rendering Hebrew arel)
etymology: From un- and the Latin circumcido, to cut around. Hebrew arel means having a foreskin, and by extension anything closed, unresponsive, or unready — a fruit tree in its first years is called uncircumcised, meaning its fruit is not yet fit.
biblical_def: Uncircumcised begins as a description of those outside the covenant sign and becomes, in the prophets, a charge against those inside it. David uses the plain sense as an insult with a theological point: “who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (1 Samuel 17:26) — the giant's size is not mentioned; his standing before God is. But Jeremiah levels the ground: “all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart” (Jeremiah 9:26). The nations lack the sign; Israel has the sign and lacks the thing signified, which leaves them in the same case and with less excuse. Stephen brings the charge into the New Testament and it costs him his life: “Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost” (Acts 7:51). The ears are added — a closed ear is as much a covenant failure as a closed heart. Moses uses the figure of his own speech: “how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who am of uncircumcised lips?” (Exodus 6:12), meaning lips not fit for the work. In each case the word marks something unready, unopened, and needing to be cut.
webster_summary: Outside the covenant sign — and in the prophets, a charge against those who bear it. Israel is uncircumcised in heart, Stephen's hearers in heart and ears, Moses in lips: what is uncircumcised is closed and must be cut.
webster_full: UNCIRCUMCISED, a. Not circumcised; not having undergone circumcision.
2. In Scripture, the uncircumcised, the Gentiles, who were not under the covenant sign.
3. Figuratively, unregenerate; not purified in heart; as uncircumcised in heart and ears, Acts 7.
4. UNCIRCUMCISION, n. The state of being uncircumcised; also, the Gentiles collectively, Rom. 2.
5. CIRCUMCISE, v.t. [L. circumcido, to cut around.] To cut off the foreskin, a rite instituted as a sign of the covenant, Gen. 17.
corruption_summary: The covenant sign is treated as sufficient in itself, so that possessing the outward mark is mistaken for possessing the reality — the error the prophets named and Paul answered in Romans 2.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah's charge is the most uncomfortable in the Old Testament for religious people, because it puts the circumcised and the uncircumcised in the same list. Paul draws out the conclusion: he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly… but he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter (Romans 2:28-29). The application to any church that practises an ordinance is immediate. Baptism does not regenerate, and a name on a membership roll is not the new birth. The Baptist conviction that the sign belongs to those who profess faith is not a small matter of order; it is an attempt to keep the sign attached to the thing signified, so that no one is comforted by a mark he does not answer to.

The principle to recover is that the cutting must be done and cannot be done by the man himself. Deuteronomy commands Israel to circumcise the foreskin of their heart, and then, thirty chapters later, promises that the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). The command and the promise stand together without embarrassment: God requires what only God can give, and the requirement is what drives a man to ask for it. Paul names the fulfilment in Colossians — a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew arel means uncircumcised, and by extension closed or unfit; mul is the verb, to cut around. Greek akrobustia is uncircumcision, used by Paul for the Gentile state.
roots_lines: Hebrew arel (H6189) — uncircumcised; also applied to heart, ears, lips, and unripe fruit.
Hebrew mul (H4135) — to circumcise, to cut around; the verb of Genesis 17 and Deuteronomy 30:6.
Hebrew orlah (H6190) — the foreskin; the fruit of a young tree is called its orlah, Leviticus 19:23.
Greek akrobustia (G203) — uncircumcision; Paul's term for the Gentile condition.
Greek peritome (G4061) — circumcision; and acheiropoietos, made without hands, Colossians 2:11.
usage: Of the plain sense, with a theological edge: who is this uncircumcised Philistine (1 Samuel 17:26).
Of the sign without the thing: all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart (Jeremiah 9:26).
Of closed hearts and ears: ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears (Acts 7:51).

And David spake to the men that stood by him, saying, What shall be done to the man that killeth this Philistine, and taketh away the reproach from Israel? for who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
Jeremiah 9:26

Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.
Acts 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Exodus 6:12
And Moses spake before the LORD, saying, Behold, the children of Israel have not hearkened unto me; how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who am of uncircumcised lips?

pos: n. (a prostitute; figuratively, an unfaithful city or people; rendering Hebrew zonah, Greek porne)
etymology: From Old French herlot, originally a vagabond or rogue of either sex, later narrowed in English to a woman who sells herself. Hebrew zonah is from zanah, to commit fornication, and the same root gives the prophets their word for spiritual unfaithfulness.
biblical_def: Harlot in Scripture names a trade and a treachery, and the Bible uses it for both a real woman saved by faith and a city ruined by unfaithfulness. Rahab is named without euphemism in both New Testament passages that commend her: “By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace” (Hebrews 11:31), and “was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?” (James 2:25). The two verses together are a compact statement of the whole doctrine of justification: Hebrews credits her faith, James points to the act that proved it, and neither pretends her past was other than it was. She appears afterwards in the genealogy of Christ. Proverbs uses the word as a warning to a young man: “there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart” (Proverbs 7:10) — the dress announces the trade, and the danger named is the subtlety, not the clothing. And Isaiah turns the term on the holy city: “How is the faithful city become an harlot! it was full of judgment; righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers” (Isaiah 1:21). The lament is that she had been faithful. Nobody mourns like this over a city that was never a bride.
webster_summary: A prostitute, and the prophets' word for an unfaithful city. Rahab the harlot is commended for faith by Hebrews and for works by James; Isaiah mourns a faithful city become one.
webster_full: HARLOT, n. [Old Fr. herlot, a vagabond.] A woman who prostitutes her body for hire; a prostitute; a common woman.
2. In Scripture, one who forsakes the true God and worships idols, Is. 1.
3. HARLOT, a. Wanton; lewd; low; base.
4. HARLOTRY, n. The trade or practice of prostitution; habitual or customary lewdness.
5. In old writers, a servant or menial of either sex; a term of reproach.
corruption_summary: Rahab's designation is sanitised out of embarrassment, and the prophetic use of harlotry for idolatry is softened — though Scripture keeps both, and keeps them for a reason.
corruption_paragraphs: Some translations and many retellings quietly upgrade Rahab to an innkeeper. The Holy Ghost did not. Both New Testament writers who commend her attach the word: the harlot Rahab, in a roll of faith beside Abraham and Moses, and in a genealogy that runs to Christ. The embarrassment is ours and the plainness is God's, because the point of naming it is that grace is not selective about where it starts. A gospel that has to tidy up its converts before it can commend them is not the gospel of a Saviour who was called the friend of publicans and sinners. The prophetic use is softened for the opposite reason. To call idolatry harlotry sounds crude to modern ears, and preaching avoids it. But the metaphor is not decoration; it carries the doctrine. God relates to his people by covenant, which is a marriage and not a contract, and unfaithfulness in a marriage is not a policy disagreement. Hosea was made to live the figure so that no one could mistake its force.

The principle to recover is the pairing of Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25, which have been set against each other for centuries and were written about the same woman doing the same thing. Hebrews says she did not perish by faith; James says she was justified by works when she received the messengers. Paul and James are answering different questions — what justifies a sinner before God, and what shows a man's claim to faith is real. Rahab hid the spies because she believed what she had heard about the LORD, and the hiding is the visible form her faith took. Faith alone justifies, and the faith that justifies is never alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew zonah is a prostitute, from zanah, to commit fornication — the same root used of Israel's idolatry. Greek porne is a harlot; porneia, fornication.
roots_lines: Hebrew zonah (H2181) — a harlot; the participle of zanah, to go a whoring.
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication; used throughout the prophets of idolatry.
Hebrew naaph (H5003) — to commit adultery; the covenant sin of a wife, applied to Israel.
Greek porne (G4204) — a harlot; the word of Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25.
Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; the general term for unlawful sexual union.
usage: Of faith commended without euphemism: by faith the harlot Rahab perished not (Hebrews 11:31).
Of the works that proved it: was not Rahab the harlot justified by works (James 2:25).
Of a faithful city fallen: how is the faithful city become an harlot! (Isaiah 1:21).
scriptures: Hebrews 11:31
By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.
James 2:25
Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?
Proverbs 7:10
And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart.
Isaiah 1:21
How is the faithful city become an harlot! it was full of judgment; righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers.

pos: a. (of the colour of snow or light; the colour of purity, victory, and glory; rendering Hebrew laban, Greek leukos)
etymology: From the Saxon hwit. Hebrew laban means to be white, and gives the name Lebanon, the white mountain. In Scripture white is the colour of what is clean, of what has conquered, and of what heaven wears.
biblical_def: White is the colour of heaven's wardrobe, and Revelation supplies most of its uses. The great multitude are identified by a paradox that no other religion could write: “These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). Blood stains; this blood whitens, and the robes are washed by those who wear them, which is faith laying hold of an atonement already made. To the church at Sardis, mostly dead but with a few names that had not defiled their garments, the promise is: “He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life” (Revelation 3:5). And when heaven opens, “behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war” (Revelation 19:11) — the colour of purity mounted for battle. Against all this our Lord sets the counterfeit: “ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness” (Matthew 23:27). Whitewash was applied to tombs so that passers-by would not touch them and be defiled. A white that is painted on warns others away; a white that is washed in makes clean.
webster_summary: The colour of purity, victory, and glory. Robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb, overcomers are clothed in white, the Faithful and True rides a white horse — and hypocrisy is whitewash over a tomb.
webster_full: WHITE, a. [Sax. hwit.] Being in the color of pure snow; snowy; not dark; as white paper; a white skin.
2. Pale; destitute of color in the cheeks.
3. Having the color of purity; pure; clean; free from spot; as white robed innocence.
4. WHITE, n. One of the natural colors of bodies, but not strictly a color.
5. WHITED, pp. Made white; whitewashed; as whited sepulchres, Matt. 23.
corruption_summary: Purity is pursued as reputation rather than as cleansing — a whitewash applied outside — and Revelation 7:14 is quoted without noticing that the whitening agent is blood.
corruption_paragraphs: The whited sepulchre is our Lord's sharpest image for religion managed from the outside, and its details repay attention. The whitewashing of tombs was not vanity but a public service: it marked graves so that pilgrims would not step on them and become unclean before a feast. The paint was a warning label. So when Christ calls the scribes whited sepulchres he is saying that their careful exterior does not merely fail to help — it advertises a danger that others should keep clear of. Reputation-management in religion always ends here, because a white applied from outside can only ever cover, and what it covers goes on being what it is.

The principle to recover is the arithmetic of Revelation 7:14, which is chemically impossible and theologically exact. Robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb. Every other cleansing agent removes a stain by taking it away; this one whitens by absorbing it, because the blood is the life of a substitute poured out for the guilt in question. This is why the doctrine of penal substitution cannot be traded for a theory in which the cross merely demonstrates love or defeats powers. Only a death that actually bore the sin can be described as the thing that makes a robe white.
roots_summary: Hebrew laban is to be white, and gives Lebanon, the white mountain. Greek leukos is white or bright; koniao is to whitewash, the verb behind whited sepulchres.
roots_lines: Hebrew laban (H3835) — to be white, to make white; though your sins be as scarlet, Isaiah 1:18.
Hebrew chur (H2353) — white linen or cloth; the hangings of the Persian court.
Greek leukos (G3022) — white, bright, brilliant; the raiment of angels and of the redeemed.
Greek leukaino (G3021) — to whiten; used of the robes washed in the blood of the Lamb.
Greek koniao (G2867) — to whitewash, to plaster; whited sepulchres, Matthew 23:27.
usage: Of robes whitened by blood: made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).
Of the overcomer's promise: the same shall be clothed in white raiment (Revelation 3:5).
Of whitewash over corruption: ye are like unto whited sepulchres (Matthew 23:27).
scriptures: Revelation 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
Revelation 3:5
He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.
Matthew 23:27
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
Revelation 19:11
And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war.

pos: a. (foreign, belonging to another; not appointed by God; rendering Hebrew zar and nokri, Greek xenos)
etymology: From Old French estrange, from the Latin extraneus, external, from extra, outside. Hebrew zar means another's, alien, not one's own; in cultic contexts it means unauthorised — belonging to someone other than the LORD.
biblical_def: Strange in the Authorized Version means belonging to another, and in worship it means unauthorised. Its gravest use is at the tabernacle's dedication: Nadab and Abihu “took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not” (Leviticus 10:1) — and fire came out and devoured them. The last clause is the whole indictment: not fire he forbade, but fire which he commanded them not. That distinction is the regulative principle of worship in a single phrase. The word also names the gods of the nations: “They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, with abominations provoked they him to anger” (Deuteronomy 32:16), and Proverbs uses it of the adulteress, the strange woman whose “lips… drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil” (Proverbs 5:3) — strange because she is another man's. And it names the exile's condition: “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psalm 137:4). The captives are not refusing to sing; they are refusing to make their worship a performance for the men who burned the temple.
webster_summary: Belonging to another; in worship, unauthorised. Strange fire is fire God commanded not; strange gods provoke him; the strange woman is another man's; and the exile will not sing the LORD's song in a strange land.
webster_full: STRANGE, a. [Fr. etrange; L. extraneus, from extra, without.] Foreign; belonging to another country.
2. Not domestic; belonging to others.
3. New; not before known, heard or seen; hence, wonderful; causing surprise.
4. Odd; unusual; irregular; not according to the common way.
5. In Scripture, strange gods, false gods; strange fire, fire not from the altar, Lev. 10.
corruption_summary: Worship is treated as an open field where anything not forbidden is permitted — the exact reverse of Leviticus 10:1, where the fatal fault was fire God commanded not.
corruption_paragraphs: The regulative principle of worship holds that what God commands in his worship is required and what he has not commanded is not permitted, and Leviticus 10 is its plainest warrant. Nadab and Abihu were ordained priests doing a priestly act with priestly equipment; the fire was not idolatrous, and no statute is cited that they broke. The text says only that God commanded it not, and that is stated as sufficient. The modern instinct runs the other way — a practice is admissible unless a verse forbids it — and it is how a great deal enters a church without anyone ever deciding to admit it. The principle is not a preference for bare services; it is a refusal to let the church determine for itself what God will accept, which is precisely what Nadab and Abihu assumed they could do.

The principle to recover is in Psalm 137, which is often misread as sullenness. The captives had hung their harps on the willows, and the demand was for one of the songs of Zion — the men who had destroyed the temple wanted the temple music as entertainment. The refusal is an act of reverence: the LORD's song is not a performance and does not belong to a strange land. There is a lesson for an age that consumes worship as content. A Christian may sing anywhere and may decline to make his worship a spectacle for those who would treat it as one, and the psalm gives him the vocabulary.
roots_summary: Hebrew zar is another's, alien, unauthorised; nokri is foreign. In worship contexts zar marks what is not appointed — strange fire, strange incense, a stranger who may not approach.
roots_lines: Hebrew zar (H2114) — strange, alien, unauthorised; the fire of Leviticus 10:1.
Hebrew nokri (H5237) — foreign, of another nation; the strange woman of Proverbs.
Hebrew nekar (H5236) — that which is foreign; strange gods in Deuteronomy 32:16.
Greek xenos (G3581) — strange, foreign, a stranger or guest; think it not strange, 1 Peter 4:12.
Greek allotrios (G245) — belonging to another; a stranger's voice the sheep will not follow.
usage: Of unauthorised worship: offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not (Leviticus 10:1).
Of the gods of the nations: they provoked him to jealousy with strange gods (Deuteronomy 32:16).
Of song withheld in captivity: how shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land? (Psalm 137:4).
scriptures: Leviticus 10:1
And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not.
Deuteronomy 32:16
They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, with abominations provoked they him to anger.
Proverbs 5:3
For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil:
Psalm 137:4
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?

pos: n. (a charge or function committed to a man; a settled position of service; rendering Hebrew pequddah, Greek diakonia and episkope)
etymology: From the Latin officium, duty or service, from opus and facio — a work done. The root idea is duty rather than dignity, which is exactly the New Testament's emphasis when it describes the offices of the church.
biblical_def: An office in Scripture is a charge given, not a rank achieved. Zacharias is found “while he executed the priest's office before God in the order of his course” (Luke 1:8) — an old man doing his appointed week when the angel came, which is where God generally finds people. Paul owns his charge without apology: “inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office” (Romans 11:13) — he magnifies the office rather than himself, and the distinction is the whole of Christian ambition. The two standing offices of the church are named in one chapter, and both are described as work. Of the first: “This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1) — and the New Testament uses bishop, elder, overseer, and pastor for one office, held by a plurality of qualified men in a local congregation. Of the second: “let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless” (1 Timothy 3:10) — and the order is deliberate. Proving comes before serving; a man is examined and only then installed. Both lists in that chapter are dominated by character rather than gifting.
webster_summary: A charge committed to a man — from the Latin for duty, not dignity. Scripture knows two standing church offices, elder and deacon, describes them as work, and requires proving before installing.
webster_full: OFFICE, n. [L. officium, from officio, opus and facio, to do work.] A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose.
2. A duty, charge or trust of a sacred nature; as the priest's office, Luke 1.
3. Business; particular employment; that which is peculiar to any one.
4. That which a thing is fitted to perform; as the office of the stomach.
5. A place or apartment in which persons transact business.
corruption_summary: Office is treated as either an honour to be claimed or a formality to be dispensed with — and the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3, which are almost entirely moral, are quietly replaced by gifting and results.
corruption_paragraphs: Read the qualifications for an elder and notice what is missing: no requirement of eloquence, charisma, education, or measurable success. The list is blameless, husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach, not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, patient, not a brawler, not covetous, ruling his own house well, not a novice, and of good report of them which are without. Only apt to teach touches ability at all. A church that selects leaders by platform presence has not merely used a different method; it has used a method Scripture declines to give. And 1 Timothy 3:10 attaches a procedure to the standard — first be proved — which takes time and cannot be done at a distance. The opposite error dispenses with office altogether in the name of organic community. Scripture will not have it: elders were ordained in every church, deacons were appointed for a specific need, and the congregation is told to obey them that have the rule over them and to submit.

The principle to recover is Paul's in Romans 11:13. He magnifies his office — not his personality, gifts, or results. That is the only form of self-regard permitted to a Christian in service, and it is a form that grows smaller as it grows louder, because magnifying an office means insisting on the weight of a charge one did not invent and cannot alter. Zacharias in Luke 1 shows the same thing without a word: an old priest at his appointed duty, in the order of his course, on the one day in his life it mattered most.
roots_summary: Hebrew pequddah is an oversight or charge, from paqad, to visit or appoint. Greek episkope is the office of an overseer; diakonia, service or ministry.
roots_lines: Hebrew pequddah (H6486) — oversight, charge, office; let another take his office, Psalm 109:8.
Hebrew kahan (H3547) — to act as priest, to minister in the priest's office.
Greek episkope (G1984) — the office of an overseer; the office of a bishop, 1 Timothy 3:1.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder; the same office as episkopos, overseer.
Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve, to minister; use the office of a deacon, 1 Timothy 3:10.
usage: Of a priest at his appointed duty: while he executed the priest's office before God (Luke 1:8).
Of the office magnified, not the man: I magnify mine office (Romans 11:13).
Of proving before installing: let these also first be proved (1 Timothy 3:10).
scriptures: Luke 1:8
And it came to pass, that while he executed the priest's office before God in the order of his course,
Romans 11:13
For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office:
1 Timothy 3:1
This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
1 Timothy 3:10

pos: a. and n. (of the sex that begets; the man as distinguished from the woman; rendering Hebrew zakar, Greek arsen)
etymology: From the Latin masculus, through Old French masle. Hebrew zakar is from a root meaning to remember or mark — the male is the marked one, and the same root gives the word for a memorial.
biblical_def: Male is one of the two terms in which Scripture states what a human being is: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them” (Genesis 1:27). Three clauses, and they must be held together — humanity is made in God's image, and that humanity exists as male and female. The distinction is creational, deliberate, and prior to the fall, and it is not a defect to be transcended. Our Lord treats the verse as settling the question of marriage: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4), and he goes on to the one flesh of Genesis 2. He appeals not to Mosaic legislation but to the creation, which is why the argument cannot be answered by pointing to changed circumstances. The law also uses the word for what belongs to God: “every firstling that cometh of a beast which thou hast; the males shall be the LORD'S” (Exodus 13:12) — the firstborn male redeemed by a substitute, pointing forward. And Paul states what the gospel does with the distinction: “there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). The context is who may be an heir, and the answer is everyone in Christ, equally.
webster_summary: One of the two terms in which Scripture defines humanity: male and female created he them. Christ grounds marriage in that creation; Galatians makes both sexes equal heirs without abolishing the distinction.
webster_full: MALE, a. [Fr. male; L. masculus.] Pertaining to the sex that procreates young, and applied to animals of all kinds.
2. Denoting the sex which begets, as distinguished from the female, which conceives and bears.
3. In botany, denoting the stamen or stamens.
4. MALE, n. Among animals, one of the sex that begets young.
5. In Scripture, male and female created he them, Gen. 1; every male shall be called holy to the Lord, Luke 2.
corruption_summary: Sex is recast as an identity chosen or felt rather than a creational, embodied, immutable category — and Galatians 3:28 is used to abolish a distinction Christ grounded in the creation.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 1:27 states that God made humanity male and female, and Christ cites it as decisive. The modern claim that gender is an inner identity detached from embodied sex is therefore not a refinement of the biblical position but a rejection of it. Scripture knows two sexes, given at creation, borne in the body, and not subject to revision; the categories of gender identity and of sex assigned at birth are themselves the corruption of Genesis 1:27, because they relocate the truth about a person from what God made to what a person feels. This must be said with compassion and without retreat: every person who is confused or in distress about this bears the image of God and is owed truth and kindness together, which is precisely what an affirming answer withholds. Galatians 3:28 is enlisted to the same end, and the verse is about inheritance. Paul has been arguing that all who are of faith are children of Abraham and heirs according to the promise, and his point is that Jew and Greek, bond and free, male and female stand on identical ground as heirs. He is not dissolving the categories; he wrote the household instructions of Ephesians 5 and the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3, which assume them throughout.

The principle to recover is that equality and order are not rivals. The same Scripture that makes man and woman equally image-bearers and equally heirs of grace also gives the creational order of headship in marriage and reserves the eldership to qualified men. These are not in competition, any more than the equality of the Father and the Son is disturbed by the Son's glad submission to the Father's will. The world can only conceive of difference as hierarchy of worth; Scripture holds equal worth and ordered roles together, and the household in which both are honoured is the one in which both husband and wife flourish.
roots_summary: Hebrew zakar is the male, from a root meaning to mark or remember; neqebah is the female. Greek arsen is male; thelus, female — the pair quoted by Christ from Genesis.
roots_lines: Hebrew zakar (H2145) — male; from a root meaning to mark, to remember.
Hebrew neqebah (H5347) — female; the counterpart term in Genesis 1:27.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — firstborn; the male opening the womb, claimed by the LORD.
Greek arsen (G730) — male; the word in Matthew 19:4 and Galatians 3:28.
Greek thelus (G2338) — female; paired with arsen in every New Testament citation of Genesis.
usage: Of the creation of humanity: male and female created he them (Genesis 1:27).
Of Christ grounding marriage in creation: made them at the beginning made them male and female (Matthew 19:4).
Of equal heirs in Christ: there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28).

So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Matthew 19:4

Exodus 13:12
